activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: The word "mediate" comes from the Latin "medius," meaning "middle," because a mediator stands between the two sides.
story:
The argument arrived before the soup did. Jessica's mother had invited Abraham and Rowan for Friday dinner because their parents were working late, and within ten minutes the two of them were glaring across the bread basket over a ruined group project. "You deleted my slides," Rowan said. "You said my part was garbage," Abraham said, gripping his fork so hard his knuckles whitened.

Jessica's father gave her a look she recognized. You fix this, it said, because he was busy carrying plates. She wanted to fix it, but she didn't want to pick a winner, because the friend she didn't pick would stop speaking to her by Monday. She remembered the vocabulary sheet from Mr. Sow's class, still folded in her back pocket. She pulled it out and smoothed it on the tablecloth between the salt shaker and her glass.

"Mediate," she read. "Comes from the Latin medius, meaning middle, because a mediator stands between the two sides." That was the whole trick, she realized. A mediator wasn't a judge. It was a position, like standing in the middle of a seesaw. So she dragged her chair around the table and planted it squarely between Abraham and Rowan, close enough that both of them had to look at her instead of each other. "Rules," she said. "Nobody talks to the other person. You talk to me. Abraham, tell me what happened with the slides, and don't say anything about Rowan while you do it."

The steam from the soup rose and the butter on the warm rolls slowly dissolved into golden pools. Abraham admitted he had clicked "delete" by accident while formatting, and Rowan admitted she had called his part garbage before checking what had actually happened. "So it's like a metaphor for the whole project," Jessica said. "You two got stretched in opposite directions, and the thing between you snapped." Rowan reached past her and pushed the bread basket toward Abraham, whose stiff shoulders finally went elastic and dropped. He tore a roll in half and handed the bigger piece across the chair where Jessica still sat.

activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
knowledge_domain: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
fact: In Lord of the Flies, the conch is smashed at the same moment Piggy is killed, which readers take as the final collapse of order among the boys.
story:
The bookshop on Miller Street had one shelf labeled "Books You Were Supposed to Read," and George had been staring at it for ten minutes. His problem was simple: Monday's assignment asked the class to track one symbol across a whole novel, and he had chosen Lord of the Flies without reading past page three. Ariel, who worked the register on Saturdays, watched him pick up the fat orange paperback for the fourth time.

"If you're going to buy it, buy it," she said. "If you're going to spy on it, that's weird."

"I need to know if the conch matters," George said. "Like, actually matters, all the way through."

Alanna appeared from behind the poetry shelf, holding a book she clearly had no intention of buying. "The conch is the shell they blow to call meetings," she said. "My brother read it twice. He says it's basically the whole book."

George bought it. At the counter he made a naive promise to himself that he would read every page, but by Sunday he had a better idea. He put a sticky note wherever the conch appeared and scrutinized each passage like a detective reading a ransom note. Calling the boys together. Whoever holds it gets to speak. Order, again and again.

Then he noticed something. The notes got darker. The conch mattered less to the boys as the chapters went on. And near the end, the sticky notes stopped mentioning Piggy and the conch separately. The shell was smashed, and Piggy was killed, in the same terrible moment on the rocks. His first assumption, that the shell was just a prop, dissolved. The conch and Piggy left the story together, and after that, nothing held the boys in line at all.

Monday morning he told Mr. Haddad his plan: trace the conch chapter by chapter and show how its power drains away until it shatters. Mr. Haddad leaned back in his chair.

"And what do you claim the shell is, George?"

George set the sticky-noted book on the desk. "Proof," he said.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When a price is kept below the equilibrium price, more people want the item than there are items for sale, and economists call that gap a shortage.
story:
The line outside the theater stretched past the bakery and around the corner, and Ella had been standing in it since 6:40 in the morning. Calvin was beside her, counting heads. "I make it three hundred and something," he said. "The website said four hundred seats, and half went to people online last night." Riya, one spot ahead, turned around. "Then there aren't enough for all of us. Some people in this line are going home with nothing."

Ella chewed on that. The tickets were fifteen dollars because the city kept them cheap for kids, and that was exactly why everyone wanted them. Last month she had skipped a different concert, telling herself she'd catch the next one, and she'd regretted it ever since. Not this time. She began to circulate through the line, walking slowly back and forth, listening. A girl near the bakery said she'd been there since five. A boy said his brother had come last year and been turned away at the window with two hundred people still behind him. A mother muttered that scalpers would be outside by noon selling the same fifteen-dollar tickets for eighty.

By the time Ella got back to her spot, she understood something she couldn't see directly. "It's a shortage," she said to Calvin and Riya. "The price is low, so way more people want tickets than there are tickets. That gap, when the price stays low like that, that's what a shortage is." Calvin frowned. "So the cheap price is why they run out?" "That's what all these stories add up to," Ella said. "Cheap tickets vanish in minutes. Remember when the pumpkin stand sold big ones for a dollar at the end of October? They had piles left and dropped the price lower just to get rid of them. Nobody wanted them, so the price fell."

At 9:02 the box office opened. At 9:31, a man in a theater jacket walked down the line calling out, "Sold out! Sold out, folks!" The word traveled toward them like a wave, and Ella watched two hundred faces ahead of her turn and drift away, some angry, some just quiet. Riya's shoulders dropped. Calvin kicked a bottle cap into the gutter.

They walked around the corner to the bus stop, and there stood Ms. Perera, their neighbor, holding three tickets she'd bought online the night before. She looked from their faces to the empty ticket window and back again. "You waited in that whole line?" Ella nodded. Ms. Perera glanced down at the tickets, then held two of them out. "My sister was my plus-one, and my candidate for the second seat just cancelled on me. You'd be doing me a favor, honestly." Ella reached out and took them before the offer could change its mind. "Riya, come on," she called. "You're not getting out of this one."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it weakens a persuasive essay rather than strengthening it.
story:
Avery spread her essay draft across the kitchen table like a detective examining evidence. The prompt was simple: persuade your reader that the school should keep the morning break. She had five paragraphs, an introduction, three reasons, a conclusion. Mr. Cohen had circled one sentence in red, the one where she wrote that kids who wanted to cancel the break were lazy. Beside it he had written a single strange word: ad hominem.

"What does that even mean?" she muttered. Kurtis, who had come over to work on his own draft, leaned across the table. He smelled like the orange he was still peeling, and the citrus scent drifted over her papers. "I got that word too," he said. "On my vending machine essay. I called the principal cheap." He tapped her circled sentence. "Look what your sentence actually argues. Does it say anything about the break?"

Avery read it again, slow this time. The sentence said nothing about the break at all. It only attacked the people on the other side. She flipped to her notes from class, where she had scribbled Mr. Cohen's example about how a strong essay targets the claim, not the person making it. So that was the pattern. Was it like hygiene for arguments, she wondered, keeping the essay clean by attacking only the idea? She underlined her three real reasons and crossed out the insult. Then a curious thought formed: if attacking the person weakened an essay instead of strengthening it, her best move was to take the other side seriously.

She rewrote the paragraph, giving the opposition a fair sentence before knocking it down with her evidence about focus and test scores. "It actually sounds smarter now," Kurtis said, reading over her shoulder. "Like you're not worried about losing."

"Maybe that's the trick," Avery said. "You sound most confident when you argue the claim itself." She was feeling optimistic enough to start a fresh draft of the vending machine essay too. Outside, a car alarm emitted a short chirp, and she laughed and put her pencil back to the paper.

activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
knowledge_domain: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
fact: The lead leg should drive over the hurdle knee first and then straighten, rather than swinging up stiff and straight, which lifts the body too high.
story:
Alexa had waited all summer for the hurdle clinic at the community pool, mostly because it meant the wooden lane markers stacked behind the diving board could finally be used for something other than tripping Tess.

"Three steps between each one," Mckinley called from the grass, where she was sprawled like a beached towel. "You're supposed to count them, not guess."

Alexa lined up the four low hurdles and went. Step, step, step, kick. The first hurdle went fine. The second one she cleared like a startled flamingo, one leg shooting up stiff and straight, and she hung in the air so long that Tess took a photo.

"Look at this," Tess said, holding up her phone. "You're floating. You look like a kite."

Mr. Gallagher, the lifeguard, leaned on the fence and laughed. "Nice hang time."

Alexa stood with her hands on her knees, staring back at the hurdle. Why did the second one feel like a slow-motion accident while the first felt quick? She ran it again and watched Mckinley's face instead of the hurdle. On the good rep, Mckinley nodded fast. On the floaty rep, Mckinley winced. Same hurdles, same grass, same three steps. Only one variable had changed, and she could deduce what it was: her leg. On every clean one, her knee came up first and then her leg straightened over the top. On every float, her leg swung up stiff, like a golf club.

Last summer's swimming lessons flashed through her mind, her instructor yelling about bent knees off the blocks, and she thought, so that's what she meant.

"Knee first," she whispered, "then straighten."

She set up again. Step, step, step, knee, snap. Hurdle one, gone. Hurdle two, gone, no floating, no kite.

"That was exceptional," Mckinley said, sitting up so fast she dropped her popsicle.

"Count it," Alexa said, already jogging back. "Three steps, four hurdles, one more time."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: Agreeing on a rule before a game starts is fairer than deciding it mid-game, because nobody yet knows whether the rule will help or hurt them.
story:
The checkers board sat on Grandma's porch table, and Bryce was about to lose. He had two kings left and Stella had four, which was when he said, "New rule. Three jumps in a row and the game is a draw." Kyleigh, watching from the railing, pointed out that Bryce already had three jumps lined up on his next turn, so his rule would save him exactly one move before Stella won.

Stella started to argue, then stopped. She thought about the rule itself instead of Bryce. If they had decided on the three-jump draw before the game started, nobody would have known who it would help, because nobody could see the future. Deciding it now, with the board already set up, was different, and she said so. "Agreeing on a rule before a game starts is fairer than deciding it mid-game, because nobody yet knows whether the rule will help or hurt them." Kyleigh said that actually made sense. Bryce tried to refute it by claiming the rule was fair for everyone, but Kyleigh nodded at the board and said, "It's fair for the guy with three jumps waiting."

Stella could see Bryce was embarrassed, and she had some empathy for him, because last summer she had flipped a whole Monopoly game off a picnic table when she landed on a hotel. So she offered him something. "We can play the next game with your rule, decided now, before anyone moves. That way it's fair." Bryce studied the board a moment, then slid a checker sideways with his king and said, "Fine. Finish this one."

She finished it in four moves. Then, before the next game, Bryce said, "Three-jump draw rule is on," and Kyleigh added, "And no changing it once we start." They both put their hands flat on the table to seal it, the way Ms. Pierre made them do when she settled arguments at the community centre. Stella set up the pieces and said, "You go first."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Instant replay was first used in a live sports broadcast by CBS director Tony Verna during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963.
story:
Emilia sat cross-legged on the living room rug between Manha and Aydan, the three of them sharing a bowl of popcorn while the rest of the family crowded the couch behind them. On the screen, the Lions were driving toward the end zone with two minutes left, and Emilia's uncle was narrating every play in a voice loud enough for the neighbors to hear. Aydan wanted the Lions to score before the pizza arrived, because he had bet his last slice on the outcome, and he kept checking the clock on the wall like the delivery guy was part of the game plan.

Then the running back lunged over the goal line, and the referee waved his arms. No touchdown. Aydan leapt up so fast he knocked the popcorn bowl sideways, and Manha shouted that the ball had clearly crossed the line, and Emilia's uncle declared that the whole call was subjective and the referees needed glasses. The announcer said the play was under review, and everyone leaned toward the television, waiting.

The replay appeared, slowed to a crawl, the ball hovering at the white line like it couldn't make up its mind. "They got it right," Emilia said suddenly. "Look at the angle. His knee is down before the ball crosses." Manha squinted at the screen, then admitted Emilia was probably right, which made Aydan groan and slide down onto the rug in defeat.

Emilia's grandfather, tucked into the armchair, nodded slowly. "You know, when I was young, TV couldn't do that. You saw it once, and it was gone." Emilia turned. "Gone? Like, no replays at all?" "None," he said. "Instant replay was first used in a live sports broadcast by CBS director Tony Verna during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963." Manha mouthed the date back to herself, testing it, and Aydan said the year like it was a math problem he actually wanted to solve.

The ruling came back: no touchdown. The clock ticked down, the Lions lost, and Aydan handed his last slice of pizza to Manha with the ceremony of a knight surrendering his sword. Emilia laughed so hard she nearly dropped her popcorn, while on the screen the stadium lights flickered and surged, the voltage dip making the picture stutter for half a second. "See?" her grandfather said, pointing at the set. "Even now, the TV has bad days."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be tested against evidence and shown to be true or false, while an opinion expresses a belief, feeling or judgment that evidence cannot prove.
story:
The argument started over the lasagna, which Lea's dad had made from a recipe Ms. Castillo had shared with the whole class. Maxim took one bite, waved his fork like a conductor finishing a symphony, and announced that it was the best lasagna in the city. Sahib shook his head. "No, it isn't. My uncle's restaurant is the best in the city, and their lasagna has three kinds of cheese. This has two."

"Three kinds of cheese is a checkable claim," Lea said, poking at her plate. "Best is just an opinion. You can't prove best." Maxim rolled his eyes so hard he nearly dropped his fork, but Sahib leaned forward. "Fine. Then count."

Lea pulled the recipe card from the shelf above the counter, where her dad kept his favorites. The tray was still warm, and the metal serving spoon resting against its edge, a good conductor, had heated up too; she used a folded napkin to nudge it aside. The three of them bent over the card while her dad laughed and kept eating. Ricotta, mozzarella. Only two. Sahib's shoulders sagged. "Okay, that part I got wrong. But my uncle's is still the best."

"That part you can't be wrong about," Lea said. "That's the whole point. Nobody can check best. But three cheeses, we just checked that. It took thirty seconds."

Maxim wasn't finished. "So if I said the cafeteria pizza is better than this lasagna, that's an opinion too, right? Nobody can test it." He mimicked Ms. Castillo's warning voice, finger raised: "One that evidence cannot prove." Sahib laughed, but then he stopped and looked at the recipe card again.

"Wait," Sahib said. "The card says nothing about basil, but I taste basil. That's another checkable claim, hidden." Lea pulled a leaf off the top of the tray and held it up to the light, thin and ragged at the edges. "My dad grows it on the windowsill," she said. "I saw him pick it an hour ago." Sahib grinned and stabbed his fork into the lasagna for another bite. "Then I claim it's delicious."

"That's an opinion," Maxim and Lea said at the same time, and her dad raised his glass of water in a toast to the only thing at the table nobody could check.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: Collecting money on Free Parking in Monopoly is a common house rule, not one of the official rules, which is why players from different homes argue about it.
story:
Thunder had rolled in over the field before the team could run a single lap, so Ms. He herded the whole squad into the classroom and dug a battered Monopoly box out of the supply cabinet. Christopher ended up at a table with Alek and two other boys from the team, and within twenty minutes the game was going well, until Alek's token landed on Free Parking and he reached for the center of the board.

"Pay up," Alek said, rubbing his hands together. "All the taxes go to the middle, remember?"

"We never put anything in the middle," Christopher said. "There's no money there."

"There should be. That's how it works at my house. It's a house rule."

Christopher leaned back and thought about last summer, when a Monopoly game at his cousin's place had ended with his cousin flipping the board and everyone going home angry. Nobody had named the problem back then. They had just shouted about being cheated, and the shouting had lasted longer than the game. He exhaled slowly and tried a different route this time.

"Okay, the problem isn't that you're lying," Christopher said. "It's that your house and my house play by different rules, and nobody said which ones we're using today." He turned the box over, found the rulebook folded inside the lid, and flipped through it while Alek watched with his arms crossed. There was nothing about paying money on Free Parking anywhere in the pages. He set the booklet on the table between them.

"So it's not official," Alek said slowly, reading over Christopher's shoulder. "It's just a house rule. My dad never told me that."

"Half the families I know play it your way," one of the other boys offered. "My grandma keeps a stack of fives in the middle."

"Then here's my idea," Christopher said. "We vote on it before we keep going, one rule for everybody, and whatever wins, that's the settlement and nobody argues after. If you want the house rule, say so now." Three hands went up for the money in the middle, so Christopher dug taxes and fees out of the bank and stacked them on the board. Alek slid his token one more space, grinned, and collected the whole pile.

"You're still going down," Alek said, counting his cash.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Hostile attribution bias is the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident.
story:
Brayden was halfway through building the ramp for his marble course in the dirt by the benches when a soccer ball plowed through it, and a second later Huxley skidded into view, arms out, laughing at something behind him. The ramp collapsed into a smear of footprints. Brayden stood up slowly, fists tight. "You wrecked it on purpose," he said. "Because I picked Fionn for the chalk contest team yesterday."

"What? No. The ball got away from me." Huxley's laugh was gone now.

"Sure it did." Brayden gathered his marbles and walked to the other side of the park, where Fionn was drawing with chalk on the pavement. Her drawing depicted a whole ocean, waves and a sea serpent with a lopsided grin, and Brayden sat down hard beside it without saying hello.

Fionn followed his eyes back across the grass, where Huxley stood alone by the ruined ramp, kicking at the dirt. "You think he did it on purpose," she said. It wasn't a question.

"He's been weird since the contest. The team picks felt random to him, I guess. Arbitrary. Like I just decided he was out."

"Or," Fionn said, "maybe it wasn't about you at all."

Brayden looked over again. Huxley had stopped kicking and was crouching down near the path where he'd been running. Then Brayden noticed it too: a patch of slick, half-dried mud right where Huxley had skidded. He got up, walked over, and stepped on the edge of it. His sneeper shot sideways and he nearly fell. The mud was like ice.

"You couldn't have stopped," Brayden said.

"Couldn't have stopped what?" Huxley said.

Brayden wiped his shoe on the grass. "I decided you meant to wreck it, and I had zero proof. Just because it was unclear, I filled in the worst thing." He frowned. "There's probably a name for that."

Mr. Wang, fixing the water fountain nearby, didn't even look up. "Hostile attribution bias," he said, and went back to his wrench.

Brayden grabbed a stick and started rebuilding the ramp, closer this time, where the ground was dry. "Hey," he called out. "You want the marbles to jump over the sea serpent?"

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: If a price is held below the equilibrium price, buyers want more than sellers will offer, and the result is a shortage.
story:
Ryan stood in the produce aisle holding two plastic-wrapped clamshells of strawberries, one in each hand, like scales. The winter ones were small, pale, and cost more than double what the summer ones had cost back in June. He wrote both prices in his notebook, then drew an arrow between them and stared at it, because Ms. He had said his class project needed to explain why, not just record that.

Simran pushed the cart into the aisle and parked it beside him. "You're doing strawberries too?" she said. "Our group picked strawberries because I want to beat Henry's group. His poster on roller coasters got the loudest applause last time, and I'm not losing to a poster of a loop." She grabbed a clamshell and turned it over, checking the sticker. "So why is it expensive now? It's just... winter."

"That's what I can't see," Ryan said. "The price is right here, but the reason is hiding behind it. I have to work backwards." He looked down the aisle. In summer, the strawberry section had been huge, crates deep, and shoppers had orbited it like planets around a sun. Now there were only three clamshells left, and a woman ahead of them took two.

Then he remembered the sale. Back in October, their class had sold strawberry cups at the fall fair to raise money for the robotics kit Simran wanted. They'd charged twenty-five cents a cup because Ryan said cheap would bring a crowd. It had. The line had stretched past the gym door, and every cup was gone in five minutes, while kids at the back of the line shouted that it wasn't fair. Simran had ended up giving away her own ticket money to a kid who cried.

Ryan stopped writing. He looked at the three winter clamshells, then at his arrow, then at Simran.

"That's it," he said slowly. "At the fair, our price was too low. When a price is below where it should be, buyers want more than sellers will offer, and you get a shortage. That's why we ran out in five minutes with that whole angry line." He tapped the notebook. "And here, in winter, it's like the price got pushed up until the few strawberries left matched how few people would pay."

Simran frowned. "So for the poster, cheap isn't always good?"

"Cheap made a shortage. I got it wrong and found out." He closed the notebook. "Ms. He says a good metaphor sticks. So the poster says: price is a dam. Hold it too low and the water floods out and the lake runs dry."

Simran picked up the last clamshell of strawberries and set it gently in the cart. "Henry's roller coaster doesn't have a dam," she said. "We're winning."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Card stacking is showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is.
story:
Willow had forty dollars of birthday money in her pocket, and she wanted the PowerTab Zoom tablet more than anything. The ad on the mall's giant screen showed five shiny features: fastest chip, brightest screen, coolest design, most apps, lightest weight. A famous actress held one up and said, "Everyone who's anyone has a Zoom." Sally stood beside Willow, nodding. "See? Five things. It must be great."

"Five great things," Willow said slowly. "But what did they leave out?" She pulled Sally toward the electronics store, where Westley was already leaning on the display case. The demo tablet was bolted down, so Willow picked up the box and read every line of fine print on the back. Battery life: four hours. Her cousin's old tablet ran ten.

"Four hours?" Westley said. "That's like half a school day."

Willow turned the box over. No mention of battery life anywhere on the front, not one word. "It's card stacking," she said. "Showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is." Sally frowned, and Willow pointed at the box. "Five great features, and the one bad fact just isn't there. That doesn't make it a lie. It makes it a really strong one-sided hand of cards."

They tested it. Willow counted shoppers who stopped at the screen ad, read the five features, and walked straight to the register. Seven people in fifteen minutes bought one, and not a single person turned the box over. "The actress said 'everyone has one,'" Sally said. "But nobody checked anything." Westley grinned. "Bandwagon plus a movie star. This mall is an entire ecosystem of tricks."

Willow put her forty dollars back in her pocket. A small radio across the aisle cost twelve dollars, and the box listed every feature and every flaw, even the cheap antenna. She bought that instead, and the resilient little thing survived being dropped twice on the way home. "You can contribute the twenty-eight dollars you saved," Sally said, "to my birthday fund."

"Deal," Willow said, and they rode the escalator down past the glowing screen, where the actress was still smiling.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: The official Monopoly rules say that if a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players.
story:
Isabelle spread the Monopoly board across the picnic table at the edge of the playground, weighting the corners with pinecones so the wind off the fields wouldn't flip it. Beyond the chain-link fence, the blades of a wind turbine turned slowly against the sky, and somewhere behind them a little kid shrieked happily down the slide. Ms. Tan, who kept an eye on the park after school, waved from her bench.

The game rolled along fine until Princess landed on Marvin Gardens. She counted her money twice, shook her head, and pushed the title card away. "I'm saving for the greens," she said. "I'm not buying it." Felix-Antoine groaned. "Then nothing happens and we all just go around again forever." He reached for the dice. Princess put her hand over them. "You can't make me buy it. That's not fair." Their voices climbed until the kid on the slide stopped to stare.

Isabelle wanted to yell too, but she made herself think instead. The fight wasn't really about Marvin Gardens, she realized. It was about what was supposed to happen after someone refused to buy, and none of them actually knew the answer. "Okay, hold on," she said. "The problem is we each made up a different rule. Let's find the real one before we fight about it." She dug the rule sheet out of the box, crumpled and coffee-stained, and smoothed it flat between the pinecones.

It took a minute of scanning, and then she found it and read it aloud: "If a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players." Princess blinked. "Auction?" "Like bidding," Felix-Antoine said, sitting up straighter. "The bank sells it to whoever offers the most."

"Then let's do it," Isabelle said, "but a fair rule first. Everyone who wants to bid gets to, and bids start at ten dollars. Nobody interrupts." They all nodded, even Princess, who was smiling now that she understood the game hadn't simply frozen around her. Felix-Antoine bid twenty for Marvin Gardens, Princess bid twenty-eight, and he went to thirty before she sat back. "Fine, it's yours. But you just spent your greens money." He laughed and handed the money to the bank.

They played until the streetlights flickered on, and when Ms. Tan called across the playground that it was getting late, Isabelle folded the board around the rule sheet so they'd never lose it again. Felix-Antoine zipped the box and handed it to Princess to carry, since her house was nearest, in the affluent streets just past the fence. "Same time tomorrow?" he asked. "Same rules," Isabelle said, and Princess answered first: "The real ones."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: A eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died; the word comes from Greek roots meaning to 'speak well of'.
story:
The church basement smelled of coffee and cough drops, and Theo sat between his mom and his friend Paityn, staring at a napkin full of crossed-out words. In twenty minutes he was supposed to stand up in the sanctuary and say something about Grandpa Ray. Twenty minutes. The program in his pocket called it a eulogy, and that word had been bugging him since Monday. "It means a speech praising a person who died," Paityn whispered, reading over his shoulder. "My mom told me. It comes from Greek roots that mean speak well of." Theo looked at his napkin. Every line he'd written complained about something: Grandpa's terrible parking, his habit of humming at movies, the way he called every dog "Steve." That wasn't speaking well of anyone.

"You look lethargic," Paityn said, poking his arm. "Like a sloth on a school day."

"I can't pick a memory," Theo said. "I have nine."

Mr. Pritchard, the pastor, leaned over from the next chair. "I once gave a eulogy with no stories at all," he said. "Worst one I ever gave. A speech without an anecdote is like soup without salt." Then he patted Theo's shoulder and went back to stacking hymnals, which was apparently how he mediated his own nerves before a service.

Theo read the napkin again and changed his mind about the whole thing. He didn't have to pick one memory. Grandpa Ray wasn't one memory; he was the parking AND the humming AND the dogs named Steve. Theo flipped the napkin over and wrote fast, printing so hard the pen tore a little hole in the paper.

When the time came, his legs felt like wet cardboard, but he walked to the front anyway. "A eulogy means speak well of," he said, "so here's the good stuff, and it's all true." He told about the time Grandpa parallel parked a van in one move, then got out and bowed. People laughed, and his mom laughed hardest, wiping her eyes at the same time. Theo kept going, napkin shaking slightly in his hand, and said, "And every dog in this town is going to miss being called Steve."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Ekadashi, the eleventh day of each half of the Hindu lunar month, is a fasting day dedicated to Vishnu on which many Hindus avoid grains and beans.
story:
Charles sat on the warm stone step of his grandmother's little house, which sat right at the edge of the cemetery where his grandfather was buried. In his hands he held a tattered wall calendar from the kitchen, one his grandmother had said she didn't need anymore. On eleven different days, faint pencil marks circled the date, and in every circle, in his grandfather's shaky handwriting, was one word: rice.

"Twice a month, he wouldn't eat rice," Charles said to Matthias, who had come along because his own mother was visiting a grave two rows over. "But the marks aren't every fifteen days. See? Here it's the eleventh, then the twenty-sixth, then the eleventh again."

They walked into the cemetery to think, past rows of headstones and a bed of marigolds that smelled sharp and sweet in the arid afternoon air. Charles counted the days between circles on his fingers, twice, three times. Each stretch ended on the eleventh day after the last one. The moon, he decided. The marks followed the moon somehow, and eleven days was where the circle landed.

His mother was kneeling at the grandfather's grave, laying a single white flower. "Dada," Charles asked, crouching beside her, "why did Nanaji skip rice on those days?" His mother smiled and brushed dust from the stone. "He called it Ekadashi," she said. "The eleventh day of each half of the lunar month. Many Hindus avoid grains and beans that day, for Vishnu." That was all she said, and it was somehow exactly enough.

"So tomorrow," Charles said slowly, "is the eleventh again." His stomach had been growling since lunch, and a small knot of resentment tightened in his chest when he thought about giving up his afternoon rice and dal. He was only ten, and half a day felt enormous. But he stood up anyway, straightened his collar, and said, "I'm going to try it. Just till sunset, like Nanaji did."

At sunset, Matthias found him back at the stone step, chewing a piece of sugarcane, which contained no grain at all. "You made it?" Matthias asked.

Charles held up the calendar, where a fresh pencil circle marked the day. "One," he said, and drew a small line beside it.

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: Where contour lines cross a stream, they bend into a V shape that points uphill, toward the stream's source.
story:
Rosalie stopped where the trail forked and flattened the map against her knees. One path climbed toward a lookout, the other dropped beside a creek, and the whole choice was written in thin brown lines she still could not read. Last summer she had abandoned a hike halfway up a hill because she'd picked what looked like the easy route and ended up on a slope so steep she had to grab tree roots. She wasn't making that mistake twice.

"Lookout," said Austin, pointing at the map. "Ms. Nair said we could pick." He wanted the view, the photo from the top, everything.

Marielle crouched beside Rosalie and pulled a small magnifying lens from her pocket, the kind her grandfather used for reading seed packets. "The lines are all squished together here," she said, holding the lens over the left fork. "And far apart here."

Rosalie traced the right-hand trail with one finger. Where the brown lines crossed the squiggle marked as the creek, each line bent. "They make little arrows," she said slowly. "V shapes. Every single one of them bends the same way." She looked up the actual creek, then down it, then back at the map. The point of each V aimed up the drainage, toward where the water came from, not toward where it was going. "So that's uphill. The water flows away from where the Vs point." Which meant the squished lines on the left fork were the steep side, and the wide-spaced lines on the right climbed the hill gradually, in long easy switchbacks.

"The left way looks shorter on the map," Austin said.

"Shorter and steeper. Like last year, when I quit halfway and you two got the view without me." She handed him the lens. "Look at the bend in the lines yourself."

Austin studied the map for a long moment, turning it so it matched the creek in front of them. He had been set on the quick route, the direct line up the barren rocky face shown on the map's western edge, because he wanted time to linger at the top before the bus left. Now his shoulders dropped an inch. "Fine," he said. "Right fork. But we're stopping at the overlook long enough for Marielle to sketch it."

They set off beside the creek, boots crunching on gravel, the water hurrying the other way. Rosalie kept the map out, matching each bend in the trail to its line, and at the first switchback she looked back down the valley and said, "Every V pointed this way."

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In Canada, the Governor General, or a deputy such as a Supreme Court justice, gives royal assent to federal bills on behalf of the monarch.
story:
Samantha pressed her nose against the courthouse window and watched rain run down the glass in fast silver lines. Her class was here for the mock legislature day, and every student had to explain one stage of how a bill becomes a law. She had drawn the final stage on her index card, but the card said only "approved," and she could not picture who actually did the approving. That was the problem. She could explain committees, debates, and votes, because those happened in rooms full of talking people. The last step happened somewhere she had never seen.

"It's like trying to count mushrooms after rain," said Nia, peeling off her wet jacket. "You can't quantify what you can't find."

"You can too," Samantha said, but her stomach disagreed. She flashed back to last month, when the class had done the forest walk behind the school and Mr. Rivera had knelt beside a rotten log. "A decomposer breaks things down so something new can grow," he had said, lifting a crumbling chunk of wood, and Samantha had thought laws worked like that too, old ones crumbling while new ones built up. Now she wondered if laws just appeared at the end, like magic.

The courtroom smelled of wood polish and old paper. A clerk led them to wooden benches that squeaked, and Samantha's card went damp and soft in her sweaty hand. Then the doors opened and a woman in a dark robe came in, and the clerk announced that a justice of the Supreme Court was attending to give royal assent to a bill. Samantha sat up so fast the bench thumped.

"That's it," she whispered. "That's my stage."

The justice spoke the words, the clerk recorded them, and the bill was law. Afterward Samantha darted down the aisle before anyone could stop her. "Excuse me. Who just approved that? I thought only the Governor General could."

"He signs on behalf of the monarch," the justice said. "But sometimes a deputy does it. Today, that was me. That is royal assent."

Samantha grinned so wide her cheeks ached. On the bus home she grabbed Nia's sleeve. "A judge can stand in. That's the part nobody in our class drew. My card said the bill just gets approved, like it's safe once it passes the vote, but it's vulnerable right up until that moment. It isn't law until assent."

"Then your card was wrong," Nia said.

"My card was a draft." Samantha held it up and flipped it over to the blank side. "Drafts get amended."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one.
story:
Ellie sat cross-legged on her bed with the tablet balanced on one knee, rereading a text from her group project. Tanya had sent her the poster schedule, and Ellie had typed back a quick reply: "Okay." Ten minutes later, Tanya answered with, "Are you mad at me or something?" Ellie blinked at the screen. Mad? She wasn't mad. She frowned at her own message, then at the kitchen doorway, where her dad was stirring soup and humming something tranquil under his breath. She scrolled up through the chat, looking for a clue, and noticed something odd. When she'd typed "okay" last week, no problem. When she'd typed "Okay." with a period, Tanya got worried. She tested it right there, sending Tanya two identical texts, one with the period and one without, then asking which one sounded upset. "The one with the dot," Tanya wrote back. "Definitely the one with the dot."

Ellie marched downstairs and out the front walk, where Mr. Rahman was pruning his roses in the afternoon light. His whole world seemed to revolve around those bushes, and he wanted one thing this spring: a bloom good enough to beat his brother's. He clipped a stem and waved her over when he saw her tablet. She showed him the two texts. "Which one sounds angry?" she asked. He squinted. "The one with the full stop. It feels like a door closing." Ellie tapped her fingers on the fence rail. It couldn't just be two people. She searched on the tablet, typing carefully, and found it: a small 2016 study by researchers at Binghamton University showed that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the exact same messages without one. She read the sentence twice, then grinned so wide Mr. Rahman asked what she'd won.

She ran back inside, found Tanya's worried message still sitting there, and deleted her half-written apology. Instead she wrote, "Not mad! The period did it. Scientists even checked." Then she copied the study sentence and pasted it in, adding at the end, "you're the best partner in the whole project dynasty, no period, no dot, nothing." Down the hall, her dad called that the soup was ready, and outside Mr. Rahman shouted, "First rose of the season, Ellie, come look!" She was already running for the door when Tanya's reply buzzed: "okay" and then, three seconds later, "okay okay okay okay."

story:

Three seats over, Lisa gasped so loudly that half the lab turned around. "MASON. You did NOT." Amanda started laughing, but Lisa was already standing, her hand halfway up to flag down Mr. Katz, who was fixing a tangled mouse cord by the door. "That's not funny," she said. "That could get you suspended."

"It's a joke," Mason said, but his stomach dropped. On the screen his words just sat there, flat and gray, exactly as serious as a real confession. Nobody could see his grin or hear his silly voice. He deleted the post, but Lisa's face stayed pinched, and he could tell a small fracture had opened in the afternoon, the kind that starts tiny and spreads if you don't do something.

He pulled up the search engine and typed "how to show a message is a joke." The first result made him blink. A computer scientist named Scott Fahlman had proposed the emoticon :-) on September 19, 1982, on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes. Mason read the date twice. People had been mixing up jokes and serious messages since before his parents were even alive, and somebody had fixed it with three little marks. He sat very still, the way he did when a pattern clicked into place, then tested his idea in the chat box: "I hid a SECOND dead fish in the drawer :-) :-)."

Amanda snorted. Lisa narrowed her eyes at him, then at the screen, then back at him. "So the fish thing was a joke?" she typed, adding her own :-) so wobbly it looked like a smile doing a cartwheel. Mason typed back, "Promise. The only thing in Mr. Katz's drawer is a chronic supply of stale mints."

By then Mr. Katz had appeared behind them, reading over their shoulders. "Dead fish, Mr. Talbot?" he said. Mason felt his ears go hot, the way only a teacher standing right there could make them. "It was a private joke, sir. Sort of public, actually. It's complicated."

"Show me this complicated fish," said Mr. Katz, and pulled a chair up to the keyboard.

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: Advertisers bid in an auction for search keywords and usually pay only when someone clicks their ad, a system called pay-per-click.
story:
Cole pushed through the door of the phone repair shop with his cracked tablet held like a pizza box. Mr. Sadeghi looked up from a half-open phone on the counter and raised an eyebrow.

"It fell off the bus seat," Cole said. "Can you fix it before Saturday? I need it for my science project." Mr. Sadeghi turned the tablet over, tapped the corner where the glass had begun to flake, and said he could, but Cole would have to find the replacement part himself because his supplier was out. "You have the shop's tablet to search on," he added, sliding it across the counter.

Cole typed screen protector into the search bar and got a wall of results. The top four all had tiny gray letters that said Ad. He was about to tap the first one when Mr. Sadeghi winced. "Careful. Advertisers bid in an auction for search keywords. They usually pay only when someone clicks their ad. It's called pay-per-click." Cole froze with his finger in the air. "Wait, so every click costs somebody money? Even mine?" "Even yours," said Mr. Sadeghi, going back to his screwdriver.

Cole stared at the screen like it was a trap with teeth. The ads looked exactly like the real results, same blue links, same bold words. He couldn't see any difference directly, so he decided to test something. He scrolled past the ads to the plain results below and started typing more specific keywords, tablet glass replacement 8 inch, then tablet digitizer Cole's model number. The ad wall shrank. When he decomposed his search into exact parts, screen size, part name, model, the ads that survived looked obviously desperate, shouting FREE SHIPPING in capital letters. The real results stayed calm and specific.

"Look at this," Cole said, pulling Mr. Sadeghi's sleeve. "The ad says 'best deals on everything.' Everything isn't a thing. The real result says exactly my part number." Mr. Sadeghi leaned in, and for the first time he looked interested instead of indifferent. He tapped the fifth result, a parts site with a big percentage off the glass Cole needed, and a phone number printed right at the top.

Cole called on the shop phone, standing on one foot, then the other. A man with a raspy voice confirmed the part was in stock and would ship that afternoon. Cole hung up and did a small punch in the air. "Two days before Saturday. I beat the deadline."

Mr. Sadeghi wrote the order number on the back of Cole's hand with a blue pen. "You found it faster than I would have," he said. Cole grinned and picked up his cracked tablet. "Same time next week? I'm going to teach Antonia and Brennan the click trap, and then we're all searching for parts for the science project." He held the door open with his shoulder. "Nobody clicks an ad without knowing it."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The term 'active listening' was introduced by psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957; it means trying to understand the speaker's point of view, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words.
story:
Quinn had spent three days not talking to Willyam, and now Mr. Bekele's classroom felt smaller than ever. The desks had been rearranged into pairs for the history project, and there was Willyam, sliding into the seat beside her, arms crossed. "You signed up with Andy for the science fair without asking me," he said. "You don't even care."

Quinn stared at the vocabulary list on her desk. The argument had started Friday, but she kept replaying it, weighing whether she had actually done something wrong or whether Willyam was just being touchy. She wanted to fix it. She just didn't know how.

Her eyes drifted to the poster Mr. Bekele had tacked above the pencil sharpener. ACTIVE LISTENING, it said. Carl Rogers and Richard Farson, 1957. Below that, in smaller print: try to understand the speaker's point of view by repeating their meaning back in your own words. Quinn had walked past that poster a hundred times without reading it. Now she turned it over in her mind. Maybe the whole fight didn't hinge on the science fair at all. Maybe it was about something underneath, and if she could name it back to him, she'd find out whether her guess was close or only an approximate one.

"So," she said slowly, "you felt like I picked Andy over you. Like he mattered more."

Willyam's shoulders dropped half an inch. He picked at the corner of his notebook. "Yeah. That's it exactly." He hesitated. "I didn't know how to say it before. I restrict myself to being mad because it's easier."

"Andy just asked first," Quinn said. "You were out sick. But next project, I'm asking you before anyone." She held out her fist.

Willyam looked at it for a second, then bumped it. "Deal. Now can we please get an A on this, because Mr. Bekele already gave me the evil eye twice?"

Quinn laughed, flipped her notebook open, and clicked her pen.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: People tend to remember the first and last items in a list best, a pattern called the serial position effect, which is why openings and closings matter.
story:
Savannah tapped her note cards against the table and watched Kristen finish a practice round in the crowded cafeteria of the tournament host school. Her own speech was in forty minutes, and it was a mess. She had a hook about her aunt's tropical garden, three points about why schools should require the flu vaccine, and a closing that was basically "so, yeah." The problem was her best point, the one about how sick classmates miss weeks of school, was buried in the middle where she kept forgetting it herself.

"Want to time you?" Martha asked, sliding into the seat beside her with a stopwatch shaped like a strawberry. Savannah nodded and stood up, launching into the hook. When she finished, Martha frowned at her notes. "I remembered your garden part and your ending," she said, "but I already lost your middle point, and I was listening on purpose. The judges won't even be trying."

Savannah sat down and stared at her cards. Maybe the order was the problem, not the words. If people's attention soaked up whatever came first and whatever came last, the way a sponge saturates only at its edges when you dip it halfway, then the middle was a dead zone no matter how good the point was. She rearranged the cards, moving the missed-schools argument to the front and the weakest point to the middle. Then she made her closing echo her opening line about her aunt's garden. "Again," she said, and Martha clicked the stopwatch.

In the round, Savannah spoke to the judge, not to her cards, and when she sat down she could tell from the judge's pen that both her garden hook and her strongest point had landed. Afterward, outside the room, Martha bounced on her toes. "I read about this once," she said. "First and last items in a list stick best. It's called the serial position effect." Mr. Kim, who had been listening from the doorway, gave Savannah a thumbs-up and held up the ballot with the top score circled twice. Savannah grabbed Martha's hand and spun her around once in the empty hallway. "Next time," she said, "we bury Martha's worst point in the middle."

Elliot wanted to beat her to it with facts instead of just his own opinion, which was that the bridge was the best fishing spot in town and should be preserved exactly as it was. The first results were just other people repeating the same sentence, which felt like cheating somehow. Then Lexie's name popped up in the chat window. "You watching the game? Did you SEE that bridge ad? It said most dangerous in the STATE." Elliot's fingers hovered over the keyboard. If he said "yeah, it's probably true," he'd lose tomorrow. Its whole purpose, as far as Elliot could tell, was taking claims apart to see if they held up, which seemed like a useful phenomenon in a world where commercials could say whatever they wanted.

He scrolled. At the top of the page was a little gauge graphic. His mom leaned over his shoulder, drying a plate. "What's that meter called?"

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: Circuit diagrams show current flowing from positive to negative, but the electrons in the wires actually move from negative to positive.
story:
Lucy pressed the switch on her science fair project for the tenth time, and the little bulb glowed steady and bright. Across the gym, Fernando slumped over his own table, where a maze of wires sat dark around a potato battery. "It worked last night," he said. "Now nothing." Lucy could see he wanted a ribbon as much as she did, maybe more, because his grandfather had driven two hours to come watch the judging. She left her diagram and walked over.

"Show me your circuit," she said. Fernando pointed at the tangle. Together they lifted wires one component at a time, the battery, the switch, the bulb, and set them out in a straight line. Lucy followed the path with her finger, the way Ms. Krause had taught her class back in September. Then she stopped. "Your switch isn't connected on one side. The loop is broken." Fernando snapped the loose wire into the clip, and the bulb lit. His whole face changed.

Then Amirah hurried over, holding a library book open to a page of circuit diagrams. "Look at this," she said. "The arrows point from the positive end of the battery to the negative one. But my brother says that's backwards. The electrons, the tiny things actually moving in the wires, go the other way, from negative to positive. The book can't be wrong, can it?"

Lucy frowned and traced the arrows in the diagram, then traced her own circuit the same direction and the opposite direction. The bulb did not care. It glowed either way, because the loop was the thing that mattered, not which way you drew it. "Maybe both are true," she said slowly. "The diagram arrows show what the book calls current, positive to negative, but the electrons really move negative to positive. Two different arrows for two different ideas." Amirah copied that into her notebook, and Fernando leaned over to clarify one part. "Wait, so when I followed your finger earlier, I was following the made-up direction?" Lucy grinned. "You were following the useful one."

Ms. Krause stopped at Lucy's table during judging and asked why her bulb lit. Lucy flipped the switch off, then on, and said, "It only lights when the loop is complete, and if you ask which way things flow, that depends which arrows you mean." Ms. Krause raised her eyebrows and made a small mark on her clipboard. Behind her, Fernando waved, his potato bulb still glowing.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Preheating means waiting until the oven has reached the set temperature before the batter goes in, so baking starts at the right heat.
story:
Julia cracked two eggs into the bowl and counted the dry ingredients Ms. Gagnon had set out on the long steel counter. At the community kitchen on Saturday mornings, each kid got one recipe card, and today hers said blueberry muffins, makes twelve. Her friend Joshua was already stirring his batter at the next station, faster than the card said, sending flour onto his sleeves.

Julia read the card top to bottom before she started. The first line said to preheat the oven to 375 degrees. She turned the dial, and the orange light beside it came on. Then she measured the flour, the sugar, the baking powder, and folded in the blueberries, keeping the batter lumpy the way the card demanded. Isabella leaned over from the cranberry station and said her oven light had gone out a minute ago, so hers must be ready.

Julia looked at her own oven, still glowing orange. She wanted to finish first, because the three best muffins of the morning got their photo on the kitchen's bulletin board by the door. So she spooned her batter into the tray, slid it into the oven, and shut the door while the light was still on. The rack felt barely warm through her oven mitt. She set the timer for twenty-two minutes and went to wash the bowls.

When the timer beeped, her muffins were pale and flat, with tops that had spread sideways instead of doming, like small planets gone wrong at the equator. Joshua's muffins, which had gone in after hers, stood up round and golden. Julia lifted one of hers out and turned it over, assessing the soggy bottom and the pale crumb. Same recipe, same kitchen, same twenty-two minutes. The only difference she could find was the light.

She looked up at the ovens along the wall. Every oven had a small light that switched off when the machine reached its set temperature, and every tray that had gone in after the light went dark had come out right. Hers had gone in while the oven was still heating up, so the batter had sat in rising heat instead of starting at the full 375 degrees. The card said to preheat, and now she understood what that meant: wait until the oven has reached the set temperature before the batter goes in, so baking starts at the right heat. She had skipped the waiting part.

Julia scraped her tray clean and started over, measuring the flour again and cracking two more eggs. This time she watched the orange light, and she did not open the oven door until it went out. She slid the tray onto the rack, and the heat rolled out over her mitts like something molten. Then she set the timer, and Isabella said, "Now you just have to hope they beat Joshua's."

The timer beeped. Julia opened the door and lifted out twelve muffins with round, golden tops, and Ms. Gagnon came over with the camera and said, "These are going on the board."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: Choral music is often written for four voice parts, soprano, alto, tenor and bass, from highest to lowest.
story:
Zoe stood at the back of Mr. Yilmaz's studio, holding her folder like a shield. In September she had chosen to stand with the altos because her best friend Amar stood there, and because the soprano line had looked scary, full of high notes that floated off the page like birds. That choice had felt temporary at the time, easy to undo later. It was not turning out that way.

"Alto line only," Mr. Yilmaz said, tapping the piano. "Sopranos, hum your part quietly, but do not abandon it."

Zoe sang her notes. The sopranos hummed theirs. Somewhere in the third bar the two lines tangled, and hers drifted upward until it wasn't hers anymore. Mr. Yilmaz stopped playing. "Again," he said, and the studio clock ticked through four more tries, each one collapsing at the same bar.

Between tries, Zoe did a quick analysis in her head. The problem appeared exactly when the soprano part moved in the same direction as hers, toward the same neighbor note. It was like her line kept following the other line out the door. So she tested an idea: she pressed one finger against her left ear, half blocking the bright soprano sound, and wrote tiny arrows in her music pointing down where the other part pointed up. It was a trick she had never seen anyone teach. It might work, or it might do nothing at all.

On the fifth try, the bar arrived. The sopranos rose. Zoe's finger sealed her ear, her arrows held her eyes, and her notes landed where they belonged. Her voice did not follow anyone.

Afterward, Amar leaned over. "You realize what you just did? You held the harmony. Also, I have news. My voice changed. Mr. Yilmaz moved me down to tenor."

"Tenor?" Zoe said. "You told me choir was two parts, us and them."

Amar laughed and pointed at the folders stacked on the piano bench. "Look inside. Four parts, soprano, alto, tenor, bass, highest to lowest. I'm the third one now."

Zoe opened a folder and stared at the four stacked lines, her old picture of the choir gone. "Then where do I actually belong?" she asked, and ran her finger slowly from soprano down to bass.
