story:
Ellie slid three quarters of a metre of ribbon across the library table and frowned at the craft flyer beside it. The winter fair's ornament booth wanted each volunteer to contribute a bow, and the instructions said each bow needed one third of a metre. Anaya leaned over from the next chair, where she was reading a news article about a corporation that had been caught selling counterfeit parts, which Ellie only half heard.

"I only brought this much," Ellie said, pinching the ribbon's end. "If I cut off a third, I don't know what's left over. Three quarters minus one third. The numbers don't match."

"So make them match," Anaya said without looking up. "That counterfeit thing is wild. This company copied every screw exactly, but the boxes were wrong."

Ellie stopped listening. Make them match. She grabbed a pencil and drew two rectangles on scrap paper, shading one into quarters and one into thirds. The shaded pieces were different sizes, so of course she couldn't just take one away from the other. Then she tried slicing both rectangles into twelve thin strips, because twelve came up in both lines. Three quarters covered nine strips. One third covered four. Nine twelfths, four twelfths. Same size pieces now. She wrote the subtraction and got five twelfths, then sat very still, because if she was wrong, she'd cut the ribbon and discover it too late.

Anaya finally looked over. "Why are you staring at it like it might explode?"

"Testing first." Ellie converted her paper strips into careful marks along the ribbon itself, counting twelfths lightly in pencil. Nine marks for what she had. She laid her finger on the fourth mark, where a third ended. Then she counted the marks beyond her finger. One, two, three, four, five.

She picked up the scissors and cut at the fourth mark, slow enough to feel her breath. The bow piece came away, and she stretched the remaining ribbon along the table. Five marks, exactly as the paper had promised. Five twelfths of a metre, enough to edge a small card for the fair.

"Anaya," she said, holding it up, "your counterfeit screws. Did the fakes still fit?"

"Perfectly," Anaya said. "That's what spooked everybody."

"Math doesn't spook me anymore," Ellie said, and tied her first bow.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed when limestone is changed by heat and pressure.
story:
The stone jars in Grandpa's cellar had no labels, only numbers, and Grandpa had offered Liam a deal: sort every rock into three boxes by how it formed, igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic, and the fossil knife on the shelf would be his by summer's end. In the garden that morning, Grandpa was yanking out a tangle of vines that had swallowed the fence whole. "This stuff is invasive," he muttered. "Came from nowhere and took over everything." Liam knelt on the cellar steps with his first handful, listening to the roots tearing.

The dark rocks with bubbles trapped inside had to be igneous; they had cooled from something molten. The layered ones split like old cake, so those were sedimentary, built up layer by layer, sometimes out of the shells of some tiny organism whose shape still ghosted through the stone. But the third jar held the trouble. Its rocks were pale, streaked like frozen cream, and none of them looked formed by anything. They looked like they had always been that way, which Liam knew was impossible. He set one aside, a chunk big as a fist, and worried at it all afternoon.

He tried to summarize his problem out loud over dinner. "I can sort the ones with bubbles and the ones with layers. It's the pale ones I can't place. Jersey would laugh at me. He went to the museum last week and came back knowing everything." Grandpa only raised an eyebrow and said the third box would stay empty until Liam stopped guessing and started testing. That night Liam lay awake, then padded downstairs and called Jersey from the hall phone, whispering so the floorboards wouldn't creak.

"You saw the statue there, right? The big white one?" Jersey said. "The guide told us it's marble, and it's metamorphic, and it started as limestone, all seabed limestone, changed by heat and pressure deep down." Liam's hand tightened on the receiver. Changed. Not formed, changed. In the morning he carried the pale chunk up to the kitchen, ran hot water over it, and pressed down with all his weight against the counter edge, watching the streaks in the stone catch the light. Then he wrote one word on the box lid and carried it down to the cellar, grinning all the way.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In East Asian dining etiquette, chopsticks should not be left standing upright in a bowl of rice, because it resembles incense offered to the dead.
story:
The wedding hall smelled like lilies and fried scallions, and Felix had one job: hold the red envelope with money for the bride and groom until the receiving line, then hand it over with both hands the way his mother had demonstrated twice in the car. Yann, whose cousin was getting married, had promised to stick next to him all evening. Ajay had come too, mostly for the dumplings.

At dinner, Felix balanced two chopsticks, a napkin, and a glass of lemonade on a crowded table. Ajay was telling a long story about a soccer ball and a garage roof, so Felix needed a free hand to eat his dumpling before it slid off the plate. He stabbed his chopsticks upright into his mound of rice and reached for the soy sauce.

The table went quiet so fast that Ajay stopped mid-sentence. Yann's grandmother, who had been laughing louder than anyone all night, set down her teacup without a sound. Yann leaned toward Felix and whispered, "You can't leave them standing up in the rice."

"Why not?" Felix whispered back, his hand frozen over the soy sauce. "It's just easier."

"Just don't. Please." Yann's face had gone pale under the paper lanterns.

Felix pulled the chopsticks out and laid them flat across his bowl, and slowly the talking started up again, though Yann's grandmother kept glancing his way. Felix's stomach stayed knotted. He had done something wrong, something big, and nobody would tell him what. He watched Yann's uncle place his own chopsticks neatly on the little rest beside his plate, and then Yann's aunt do the same, and he began to see a pattern. Nobody at the long table, not one of the forty guests, ever left chopsticks pointing straight up out of food.

He decided to petition Yann directly, out in the hallway by the coat rack, away from the ears of the relatives. "You have to tell me what I did," he said. "I'm not being obstinate, I just can't fix it if I don't know."

Yann checked that the hallway was empty. "Standing chopsticks in rice look like incense offered to the dead," he said quietly. "That's why we never do it. At funerals, that's what it means."

Felix thought about the quiet that had dropped over the table, and about Yann's grandmother and her teacup, and it all fit together like a puzzle snapping shut. He went back in, walked to the grandmother, and bowed the way he'd seen the other guests do in the receiving line, both hands pressed together. She studied him for a long moment, then patted the chair beside her.

"Eat," she said, pushing the dumpling platter toward him. "The tall boy talks too much, and the dumplings go extinct fast."

Ajay opened his mouth to argue, and Yann kicked him under the table, and Felix picked up his chopsticks and held them the way Yann's uncle did.

activity: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
knowledge_domain: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
fact: In an orchestra, the oboe usually plays the reference A that the other instruments tune to before a concert.
story:
Mr. Hu plucked one string on his guitar and let the room go quiet. "That is your reference note," he said. "In an orchestra, the oboe usually plays the reference A that all the other instruments tune to." He pointed at Jordan. "Your job is to match your E string to my A. Listen, then turn the peg a little and listen again."

Jordan held his guitar and plucked the string. The sound wobbled, like two notes arguing with each other. He tightened the peg, but the wobble only got faster. He tried the other way, loosening it, and the wobble slowed, then spread out until only one clean note was left. So the faster the wobble, the further off he was. He tested the idea by loosening too far on purpose, and the arguing came back. He tightened until it vanished again.

Kiara leaned over from the next chair. "How did you do that so fast? I've been turning mine forever." She held up her guitar. Her string was flat, and when she plucked it alongside his, he could hear the slow roll of mismatched notes.

"That's it, you're close," Jordan said. "Just tighten it a tiny bit." Behind them, Sheldon had stopped pretending to tune at all. He was watching the window, where afternoon light refracted through his water bottle and laid a crooked rainbow across the music stands. "I already know how to do this," Sheldon said, but his pegs hadn't moved once.

After class, Sheldon caught Jordan at the door. "Can you keep a secret?" His voice was abrupt, low. "I can't hear the wobble. At all. I went to the doctor last week. Something with my ears." He looked at the floor. "I didn't want Mr. Hu to take me out of the group before the concert."

Jordan thought for a second. "Don't tune by ear, then. Use the electronic tuner on my phone, every time, before anyone notices. Nobody checks how you got there." He pulled out the tuner, and its needle swung left, right, then stopped dead in the middle, right on the A. "There," he said. "Pluck it again."

activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
knowledge_domain: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
fact: In Suzanne Collins's The Hunger Games, published in 2008, Madge Undersee gives Katniss a mockingjay pin before Katniss goes into the arena.
story:
Sophie spread three crumpled sticky notes across the library table and glared at them as if they had insulted her. Her book club met in forty minutes, and Peyton had promised to bring the popcorn, which meant Sophie was responsible for everything else, including the analysis she had sworn she could do. "The mockingjay," she whispered to the open copy of The Hunger Games in front of her. The problem was that the pin showed up as a tiny moment at the start, when Madge Undersee gives Katniss the mockingjay pin before Katniss goes into the arena, and then somehow it turned into the biggest thing in the whole series. How did a small gift grow that much weight?

Violette slid into the chair across from her, smelling of rain and mint gum. "You look like you're being transported to prison." She tapped the book. "That's the one with the birds, right?"

"The mockingjay pin. Madge gives it to Katniss in chapter one, and by the end it means a whole rebellion." Sophie flipped pages, hunting. "I want to prove it changes, not just say it does. I thought I could mark every time the pin or the bird shows up and see what it means in each place." She smoothed a fresh sticky note flat. "Like checkpoints."

Ms. Byrne wheeled her book cart past and paused. "Presentation at four?" she asked, glancing at the clock above the paperbacks. Sophie nodded, throat tight. Twenty-eight minutes. Violette grabbed a pencil and started scanning the middle chapters aloud while Sophie wrote: pin, token of home; mockingjay, something the Capitol never meant to exist; mockingjay, a girl defying them anyway. When they laid the notes in order down the table, the pattern showed up like footprints in snow. The pin began as protection, a piece of District 12, and each time it returned it had gathered another layer until it stood for everyone who refused to be controlled.

Peyton burst through the doors at 3:52 with a grocery bag of popcorn and zero apologies. The four other club members gathered around, and Sophie stood, hands slightly shaky, and walked them down the line of notes like a trail. When she finished, nobody spoke for a second, and then a boy in the back said, "So Madge basically handed her a revolution in chapter one and didn't know it."

"Exactly," Sophie said, and Violette raised the popcorn bag like a trophy.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym, and a name outsiders use for it is an exonym; Germans call their country Deutschland, while English speakers say Germany.
story:
Savannah taped the last flag to the community centre wall and stepped back to check her display for the heritage night. She had made labels for every family on the sign-up sheet, and one label bothered her: "Germany," printed in neat block letters for the Brandt family. Mr. Brandt had signed the sheet himself, and she had copied it exactly, but last week he had said something odd while helping set up tables. "You know we call it Deutschland at home," he had said, laughing, and then walked off before she could ask what he meant.

She found Khaled and Emiliano stacking paper cups by the juice station. "When your family talks about Egypt, what do they call it?" she asked Khaled.

"Misr," he said. "Never Egypt. My grandma says Egypt is what other people call it."

Emiliano frowned. "So there are two names for every country? The one the group uses and the one outsiders use?"

"There's a word for it," Khaled said. "A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym, and a name outsiders use is an exonym. My sister taught me that in geography. Like Deutschland and Germany."

Savannah wanted to be sure before she changed her whole display, so she tested it like a tiny algorithm: ask the person, write the answer, compare. She went table to table with her clipboard. The woman from Thailand said "Prathet Thai." The grandfather from Greece said "Ellada." Mr. Brandt confirmed Deutschland again and grinned. It was risky to redo the labels an hour before the doors opened, maybe even reckless, but if she left them wrong the whole wall would tell a story about outsiders instead of the families themselves.

She printed new labels and taped them beneath the old ones, so both names showed. When the families arrived, they stopped at the wall. Khaled's grandmother touched the word Misr and said something to him in Arabic that made him laugh. The Greek grandfather stood in front of "Ellada" for a long moment. "This is how it should be," he said, and wrote his name on the sign-in sheet beside it.

By the end of the night the room was loud with people comparing labels, teaching each other pronunciations, arguing gently about spelling. The event had never drawn a crowd like this before; Ms. Anderson, who ran the centre, said the bulletin board club would thrive if they kept this up. Savannah peeled off the old English-only labels and dropped them in the recycling bin. "Next time we start with the endonyms," she said, and clipped the blank labels back onto her clipboard.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Joshua slid his math homework under the placemat before his father carried the spaghetti to the table. On the small kitchen TV, a replay of the hundred-meter final was frozen at the finish, and the silver medalist's face filled the screen. "Second place," his father said, spooning noodles. "He must have been way behind." He had spent the whole afternoon insulating the attic pipes and his arms were still gray with dust.

Joshua leaned closer. The two runners had crossed almost together, so close the announcer had said the gap was less than a blink. "He was only a hundredth of a second back," Joshua said. "A hundredth. That's nothing." His father shrugged and said second was still second. Something about that bugged Joshua all through dinner. Being second could mean losing by a hundredth of a second, but it could also mean losing by a whole minute. The ranking told you who was ahead, and nothing about how far ahead. He decided that wasn't good enough, and it seemed logical to test it.

He grabbed the kitchen stopwatch and a notebook. "Everybody clear your plate, starting now." His mother laughed but picked up her fork. Joshua timed each of them and wrote the numbers down: Mom 41 seconds, Dad 39, himself 53. The next night he did it again, and again the night after, so nobody could say one slow dinner ruined the results. By Friday he had a whole column of times, like a tiny census of plate clearing, and he added them up and divided to get each person's average.

At Friday dinner he pushed the notebook into the middle of the table. "Rankings," he announced. "Dad, you're first. Mom, you're second. But look." He turned the notebook so the columns faced his parents. "Dad's average is 38 seconds and Mom's is 39. One second apart, basically tied. Second place here is like that runner's hundredth of a second." Then he flipped to the row from Tuesday, when his mother had stopped to answer the phone and taken 71 seconds. "But that night, second place was a whole minute behind first. Same ranking both times. Totally different race."

His father set down his fork and read the columns twice. "So when the news says we're second in the league," he said slowly, "we might be a whisker behind or miles behind." "Exactly," Joshua said. "You have to ask for the numbers." His mother raised her water glass. "To the champion," she said, "by one single second." Joshua grinned and clicked the stopwatch one more time, just to hear it beep.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Signposting words like 'first', 'second' and 'finally' tell listeners where they are in a speech, because they cannot flip back a page the way a reader can.
story:
Penelope stood on the painted wooden stage of the community theatre, index cards shaking in her hand, and watched her grandmother's face go blank in the third row. "Two minutes on why the theatre needs a costume sale," Mr. Kerr had said, "opening hook, three points, closing, by Friday night." Penelope had rehearsed the opening hook a dozen times in front of her mirror, and it worked, because her grandmother leaned forward when she described a velvet cape from 1987 that smelled like somebody's attic. But halfway through, her grandmother whispered to Mom, "Which point is she on now? Is this the second thing or the third?"

After practice, Terrance was waiting in the aisle with his own cards. He had been meticulous about his speech, numbered cards in a rubber band, and he shook his head. "Your problem is you need a stronger hook," he said. Penelope disagreed, but she couldn't say why, so she sat on the stage edge and thought. When she read her speech to herself, she never got lost. She could flip back a card, reread a line, find her place again. Her grandmother couldn't. A listener had no pages to flip back through, so once she lost the thread, it was gone. That had to be the real hinge the whole speech turned on, not the hook.

She tested it that evening. "Grandma, I'll say it again, exactly the same, but this time I'll say 'first', 'second' and 'finally' before the points." She gave the speech on the back porch, word for word the same except for those three words, and her grandmother nodded along the whole way. "First, the storage room is overflowing," Penelope said, and her grandmother's eyebrows rose like she'd been handed a map. Terrance, sprawled on the porch swing doing his own rehearsal, looked up. "Oh," he said slowly. "It's not my hook either. My brother got lost too." He changed his mind on the spot and pulled out a pencil. "What's that called, the first, second, finally thing?"

"Signposting," Penelope said, "like street signs for your ears."

Friday night, the theatre seats filled. Mr. Kerr stood at the back with a stopwatch. Andrea went first, then Terrance, who planted his signposts firmly and didn't lose a single listener. When Penelope stepped into the lights, she found her grandmother in the third row and took a breath. "First," she said, and watched the whole audience lean in. "The storage room is overflowing."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: During puberty the larynx grows, and a boy's singing voice typically drops by about an octave, which can move him to a different choir part.
story:
Brody had sung the high part in the junior choir at the temple for three years, and he liked standing beside James, who hit every top note like it was nothing. Then, on the first Thursday of October, his voice cracked in the middle of a psalm, right on a note he had sung a hundred times. The sound that came out was somewhere between a squeak and a groan. James did not laugh. Karter, two rows back, did not laugh either, though his shoulders shook once before he got them still.

Mr. Patel, the choir director, called a break and walked over. "Brody, sing that line again. Just for me." Brody tried, and this time the note came out, but it felt like carrying a suitcase up stairs that used to be flat. Mr. Patel nodded slowly. "During puberty the larynx grows, so a boy's singing voice usually drops by about an octave. That often moves him to a different part." He said it the way he said everything, calm and quick, like a weather report. "Try the lower line with Karter for a few weeks."

Brody wanted to confess that he hated the idea, because the lower part wove against the high part, and if he drifted, everyone would hear it. Instead he shrugged and moved back two rows. The melody he knew so well now belonged to other people, and his new line seemed to wander off on purpose, like a dog that ignored whistles.

He decided to test an idea. At home he hummed the high part into one ear, using a recording on his tablet, and sang the lower part out loud over it. At first the high part grabbed him and dragged his voice upward every few bars, like a tide. Nobody was immune to that pull, he discovered; even Karter admitted that when the choir split into two parts, his own notes sometimes slid toward James's. So they practiced the trick together at recess, Karter singing the tune while Brody held the lower line, both of them getting it wrong and laughing and trying again.

By the third Thursday, something shifted. Brody's low line settled under the melody like a floor under a room, and when James's part rose, his own stayed put. Mr. Patel raised both hands for the split section, and the two lines crossed and crossed and neither one wobbled. Afterward, at the snack table, Karter passed over the cookies with peanuts without being asked, because everyone knew about his allergy, and handed Brody the plain ones.

"You sound good down there," James said. "Like a whole different instrument."

"Give it a year," Brody said, pointing at him with his cookie. "Your turn is coming."

James opened his mouth to argue, and a small crack came out instead. Karter's laugh rang all the way to the sanctuary doors.

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: Two notes a third apart, such as C and E, sound smooth together, which is why a harmony line often runs a third below the melody.
story:
Edouard stood in his grandfather's music room, holding the alto sheet music like it might bite him. The choir concert was in two weeks, and Ms. Novák had said his part needed to be steady, not just guessed at. Every time he sang the harmony line alone it sounded fine, but the moment the melody came in, his voice slid upward to follow it, like a magnet was pulling him.

His grandfather's old piano sat against the wall. Edouard had never really played it, but he knew where middle C was, because his grandfather had shown him that much. He pressed the C key, then hummed his note from the sheet music. Wrong. He checked again, and found his note two keys down, on the A below. He pressed both keys together and listened. The sound was smooth, almost like one fat note instead of two separate ones. He pressed other pairs to compare. C and the key right beside it sounded scratchy, sour. C with the key two down sounded settled, like they belonged together. So that was the trick. His alto note sat under the tune, two letter names below, which his cousin Prisha called a third apart when she texted him that evening.

"Wait, so your whole line is just a third under the melody?" Prisha wrote.

"Not all of it, but a lot," Edouard typed back, and then he tested it, playing the tune with one hand and hunting for his harmony notes with the other. Some places the rule coincided with what was written, and some places it didn't, but even where it differed, he noticed the harmony line still liked to hover just under the tune. It wasn't a strict equation he could plug notes into, like in math class. It was more like a versatile shadow that shifted but stayed close.

The next morning his grandfather sat in the doorway drinking coffee while Edouard practiced. When Edouard slipped and drifted up to the melody, he stopped, found the piano key, and pulled his voice back down under. He did it again and again, until holding his part felt less like fighting and more like standing still while someone walked past him.

At Thursday rehearsal, Ms. Novák split the choir in half. The sopranos lifted the melody into the air, and Edouard planted his note beneath it, steady, a smooth third below. For the first time, the two lines braided together without him tumbling out.

"Edouard," Ms. Novák called across the room, "whatever you did this week, keep doing it."

He grinned and held the next note even longer.

activity: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
knowledge_domain: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
fact: A doctor may give a tetanus shot after a deep or dirty wound, because tetanus bacteria live in soil and dust.
story:
The cut on Cole's palm had stopped stinging, but the memory of it hadn't. He sat on the bench at the bus stop with his hand wrapped in a paper towel, waiting for the 4:10 with Lola, who was staring at the reddish line across his skin like it might move.

"It was a rusty trowel," Cole said. "At my grandma's, in the garden shed. I reached past a spiderweb and grabbed the wrong end."

"You grabbed a rusty trowel." Lola unwrapped her backpack and dug out the little first-aid pouch her mom made her carry, which Cole used to tease her about. Now it looked like treasure. "Grandma didn't take you to a doctor?"

"She put a bandage on it. That was yesterday. Then this morning she called my mom and said maybe a doctor should look at it after all, because it was deep, and because rust means dirt." He frowned at his palm. "She said something about dirt. I didn't get it."

Lola peeled the backing off a bandage and handed it to him, then sat on her hands, which was her way of saying your turn. Cole positioned it crooked, lifted it, and smoothed it down again, gentler, so it lay flat across the cut without sticking to the red part. Lola nodded once, like a judge.

The neighbor from the blue house, Ms. Mansour, came down her walk with a grocery bag and paused at the stop. "Bandaging practice?" she said. "Good skill. I was a nurse for thirty years."

Cole held up his hand. "If it's from a rusty thing, is that bad? Like the rust itself?"

"It's not the rust, it's what's in it," Ms. Mansour said. "Tetanus. Tetanus bacteria live in soil and dust. That's why a deep or dirty wound can mean a doctor visit. Sometimes you get a tetanus shot, just in case." She checked the crosswalk, then looked back at him. "Deep or dirty, remember. A paper cut, no. A hole from a nail in a garden bed, yes."

Cole turned that over. So the rust was only a warning sign, the way smoke meant fire somewhere you couldn't see. The trowel had lain in soil, and soil held these bacteria, and the bacteria could be sitting in the cut right now, invisible, which was exactly why the wound needed more than a bandage. Grandma had figured that out overnight, he realized. Yesterday she'd dismissed the idea of a doctor, and this morning she hadn't. He wondered how often she changed her mind like that, quietly, before telling anyone.

"My mom made me a deal," he said. "I go to the clinic after she picks me up, and she takes me for dumplings after. It wasn't even voluntary. She just said, you're going."

"That's not a deal, that's a treaty," Lola said. "You get dumplings either way."

The bus rounded the corner, brakes hissing. Cole stood, pressed the bandage flat one more time, and picked up his backpack with the good hand. "Tell me tomorrow if you get the shot," Lola called after him, and he raised his wrapped palm out the window as the doors closed.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
story:
Sebastian had come to Aniya's house to work on their language arts project, a poster comparing a book with its movie adaptation, but so far the poster was blank and Aniya was holding a dress. "It came this morning," she said, lifting a white dress with a translucent overlay from a tissue-lined box. "From my aunt in Vancouver. I'm wearing it to the family thing on Saturday. My cousin's getting married, I think. Or something."

Asia, who was sprawled on the rug sketching a movie poster, squinted at the dress. "It's very white." From the kitchen doorway, Aniya's grandmother looked at the dress too, said nothing, and went back to washing rice. Sebastian noticed that, because he noticed things like grandmothers going quiet.

He kept noticing. On the fridge hung a calendar with Saturday circled, and beside the circle someone had drawn a small incense stick. On the mantel sat a photograph of a man Sebastian had never seen before, framed in black, next to an old wedding photo of Aniya's grandparents in which the bride wore red, brilliantly red, embroidered with gold. Aniya had once told him her family was Chinese on her grandmother's side, and that the man in the black frame was her great-uncle, who had died in the spring. Sebastian had an idea forming, and ideas, in his experience, were like splinters: better extracted early.

"Can I see the card that came with the box?" he asked. Aniya dug the envelope out of the trash and handed it over. He pulled out the card and read it. It was not an invitation to a wedding. It was an invitation to a memorial gathering for the great-uncle, with a time, an address, and a line about honoring his memory. Aniya read it over his shoulder and sat down on the coffee table, slowly, the way you do when a floor turns out to be softer than expected.

"So the dress," she said. Her grandmother came in drying her hands, and when Aniya held it up, the old woman nodded once. "White is what we wear for mourning," she said, and patted the fabric like it was a cat. Asia raised her hand from the rug as if they were in class. "Weird, because my cousin got married last month and her bride wore white. Big puffy white dress. Whole church full of it."

"Same color, opposite jobs," Sebastian said.

Aniya looked at the dress, then at the red bride on the mantel, then at the dress again. "Fine," she said. "But I'm wearing it to the memorial, not to any weddings. For weddings I'm borrowing your red hoodie, Asia, and that's final."

"You don't have to decide tonight," Asia said, and went back to her sketch, where the movie monster was wearing, of all things, a veil.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: Paying only the minimum on a credit card means much of each payment goes to interest, so paying off the balance can take years.
story:
Sadie sat on the hard chair beside her dad at the bank, swinging her feet and staring at the flyer in her hands. It showed a purple mountain bike for one hundred and eighty dollars, and she wanted it so badly her teeth ached. Her dad was at the counter asking about his credit card, and Sadie leaned forward when she heard the cashier say the words "minimum payment."

"Dad," she whispered when he came back, "why not just pay the little bit? The small number looks friendlier."

Her dad rubbed his forehead. "That's the trap I'm in. I've been paying the minimum for ages and the balance barely shrinks. Much of each payment goes to interest, so paying it off could take years. Years, Sadie. For a grill I barely use."

Sadie blinked. She thought about that all the way to the car. The money he sent each month was like water poured into a bucket with a hole in it, except the hole was invisible, which made it worse. Was there a ratio hiding in there somewhere, a secret comparison between the part that actually paid off the bike, or the grill, and the part that just vanished? She wanted to see it for herself.

At home she spread notebook paper across the kitchen table. Her friend Sara came over, and Isa joined her through a video call, his face pixelated on the tablet. "I'm testing an idea," Sadie announced. "If Dad had saved up first, he'd have paid one hundred and eighty dollars, once, and then owned the thing. With the card, he pays and pays, and the debt just sits there like it's too frail to die but too stubborn to leave." Sara laughed so hard she knocked over the glue.

They made two columns. Saving column: bike money set aside each week, total cost fixed. Borrowing column: minimum payments stretching on and on, years of them, and at the end Dad would have paid way more than the grill ever cost. Isa held up a hand-drawn chart to his camera, a wobbly bar graph titled "The Hole in the Bucket." Sadie decided she could monitor her own plan instead: five dollars a week from walking the neighbor's dog, plus birthday money, and the bike would be hers by spring.

The next Saturday she marched back to the bank with her dad, holding her envelope of dog-walking cash. She asked the cashier to open a savings account, and when the woman asked if she had any questions, Sadie slid her notebook across the counter, hole-in-the-bucket chart and all.

"That's my plan," she said. "Is the ratio right?"

The cashier studied it, then grinned. "Kid, you just drew the best chart I've seen all year. Let's get you that account."

fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
Levi sat in the game lobby waiting for the countdown, but his mind was on the email he had to send after the match. He wanted to invite his whole class to an online tournament on Saturday, and Mr. Sok had helped him get a list of everyone's addresses. The trouble was that his first attempt, a practice one, had put all the addresses where everyone could see them. Maiya had noticed right away. "You just showed the whole class my address," she said in the lobby chat, and the chat was public, so everyone in the waiting room saw that too. Stefan added a row of laughing faces.

Levi typed "my bad" in the lobby and then turned to the options on the side of the screen, which were private, meant for adjusting his controls, not for talking. He liked that about the lobby. Some things were broadcast, like the countdown clock and the team names, and some things only he could see, like his ping and his settings. The email program had to have something like that too, and he meant to find it before the match started.

Below the To line there was a Cc line and then a third line labeled Bcc. He had skipped it before because it looked like a typo. He clicked it open, dropped Maiya's address into the To field as a test, put his own and Stefan's into Bcc, and wrote one sentence: "Test, reply if you can see anyone's address but mine." Then the match loaded and he set the email aside, because the lobby was filling and he needed to be competent at the game too, not just at invitations.

After the match, which his team lost narrowly, he opened his inbox. Maiya had replied, "Only yours." Stefan had replied with a single question mark. So that was the rule: people added in the Bcc field received the message, but other recipients could not see their addresses. Blind carbon copy, Maiya had written in the lobby afterward, when someone accused Levi of hoarding the secret. He sent the real invitation with every address in Bcc, all forty-three of them hidden from each other.

On Saturday the tournament bracket filled up fast. When one classmate tried to accuse another of inviting a ringer from another school, Levi offered a settlement: the ringer could play, but only on the youngest team. Mr. Sok, watching from the couch with his own controller, gave a slow nod. "Round two," the lobby announced, and Levi hit ready.
